messages.author: 35a15536b9cb2cf9
messages.subject: dChip in aroma.affymetix and affy
parts:
Hello,

I am sorry for the massive email again.

I want to thank Mark for the kind help again. Thanks for the tip on
taking log2 of expression values. About saving gene expression values
part - I should have figured it out by myself and I am sorry about
that.

With all your kind help, I came up with (and understand :) ) the code
below and just started running it as script for over 2,000 arrays in a
workstation. It's been running more than an hour so far.


##### RMA normalization ######

# Loading The Package
library(aroma.affymetrix)
verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(-8);
timestampOn(verbose);

# setting up annotation files
chipType <- "HG-U133_Plus_2"
cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType(chipType)

# define Raw Data
cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("expO", chipType="HG-U133_Plus_2")

# quality assessment of raw data
postscript("OriginalPlot.ps", width = 1440, height = 900)
plotDensity(cs)
dev.off()

# background correction
bc <- RmaBackgroundCorrection(cs)
csBc <- process(bc, verbose=verbose)

# quantile normalization
qn <- QuantileNormalization(csBc, typesToUpdate = "pm")
csBcQn <- process(qn, verbose=verbose)

# summarization of probe-level data
plmRMA <- RmaPlm(csBcQn)
fit(plmRMA, verbose=verbose) # takes time

# chip effects
chipRMA <- getChipEffectSet(plmRMA)

# save RMA gene expression values
geneSumm <- extractMatrix(chipRMA, returnUgcMap=TRUE)
geneSummLog2 <- log2(geneSumm)
rownames(geneSummLog2) <- getUnitNames(getCdf(chipRMA), units =
attr(geneSummLog2, "unitGroupCellMap")[,"unit"])
write.table(geneSummLog2, file = "RMA.txt")

In affy page 10 at http://www.bioconductor.org/packages/2.2/bioc/vignettes/affy/inst/doc/affy.pdf,

R> eset <- expresso(affybatch.example,
normalize.method="invariantset", bg.correct=FALSE,
pmcorrect.method="pmonly",summary.method="liwong")

Also, from http://www.bioconductor.org/packages/2.2/bioc/vignettes/affy/inst/doc/builtinMethods.pdf

it seems that I should do (1) background correction: pass, (2)
normalization: use invariantset, (3) summary: use MBEI. I searched the
past mailing list, and it seems that invariantset is not yet in our
aroma.affy package.

The code below seems to be doing step (3) only to further get gene
expression values from http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/probe-level-modelling.

plm <- MbeiPlm(cs)
fit(plm)
ces <- getChipEffectSet(plm)

What's the difference compared to the dChip method in affy? Also, do
we have like pmcorrect.method="pmonly" in affy's RMA?


Thank you all very much in advance for your help. I hope some day, I
can be of help to other new comers in the group.

Hailong

Correct, the invariant-set normalization method is not implemented in
aroma.affymetrix. It is probably not hard to write a wrapper around
affy::normalize.invariantset(). Note that that would reproduce what
'affy' does, but only dChip approximately. This is because the
Bioconductor implementation of the dChip methods are reverse
engineered and reimplemented by reading the dChip papers, but not
ported from dChip source code.

>
> The code below seems to be doing step (3) only to further get gene
> expression values from http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/probe-level-modelling.
>
> plm <- MbeiPlm(cs)
> fit(plm)
> ces <- getChipEffectSet(plm)
>
> What's the difference compared to the dChip method in affy? Also, do
> we have like pmcorrect.method="pmonly" in affy's RMA?

The MbeiPlm class uses the affy::fit.li.wong() internally, so the
model estimates are identical. The MbeiPlm (just like RmaPlm) uses
only PM probes by default, so that is already taken care of. You can
change this behavior by setting argument 'probeModel', cf.
help(ProbeLevelModel).

Hope this helps

Henrik

On Sun, Aug 10, 2008 at 3:27 PM, Hailong <Hailo...@asu.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi Henrik,
>

>
> I have a difficulty understanding 'It is probably not hard to write a
> wrapper around affy::normalize.invariantset().' Is there any way you
> can explain a bit more details?

I mean that it is rather easy for someone who knows how
aroma.affymetrix works. A "beginner" need to get familiar with
aroma.affymetrix first and how it is designed. The code is the
description you're looking for; I unfortunately don't have the time to
guide you through it. I can only say, it's probably worth it.

>
> Also, I ran the RMA scripts in the same workstation, and it was still
> running after 24 hours so I killed the process. justRMA() in affy ran
> for 2-3 hours for the same 2,035 CEL files. Any reason you can think
> of?

The good thing is that you can restart again and aroma.affymetrix will
pick up where you interrupted it ;)

The design of aroma.affymetrix is to store all estimates to file. It
is done after each chunk of units are fitted. The more arrays the
smaller each chunk is, but you can increase the chunk size by
increasing argument 'ram' (defaults to one) of fit(). That will
decrease the I/O overhead a bit, but use more memory. In any case,
the memory usage will be constant regardless of the number of arrays
you use.

If you look at the 'verbose' output, you will see an "Estimate To
Arrivate" (ETA) after each chunk. That will give you a feeling how
long it will take to fit all.

More over, are processing data over a shared file system? There is a
penalty of doing that because of the frequent file access. This has
been observed and discussed on the mailing list before. Please
search the archive.

I know a few things that can speed up the processing, but that is not
on my top priority list (other things are more important). Also put
processing speed of that many arrays in perspective - how long did it
take to produce all those hybridizations ;)

Cheers

Henrik
